newsitem.title: UK: UK futures still see rates pressure after budget.
newsitem.headline: UK futures still see rates pressure after budget.

text.p: British interest rate futures nudged ahead on Tuesday, only tentatively scaling back expectations for imminent monetary tightening after Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke delivered his November budget.

Analysts said a package including reasonable fiscal austerity but an over-ambitious inflation target gave short sterling markets mixed signals and was not enough to calm interest rate concerns altogether.
"The market is not going to be deterred from its view that interest rates will have to rise next month," said said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Investment bank in London.

Short sterling futures cautiously edged down expectations for interest rate rises, pricing in a little over a quarter point of monetary tightening by March. March short sterling ended Tuesday's trade at 93.35, up four basis points on the day.
Before the budget speech, market expectations were for three-month money to be 32 basis points nigher by March 1997.
A general election must be called in Britain by May 1997.

Clarke reduced the pressure for interest rate rises with a deep cut in his forecast for government borrowing in the next fiscal year, slicing his public sector borrowing requirement forecast for 1997/8 to 19.0 billion sterling from a previous prediction of 13.2 billion sterling.
"I am tightening fiscal policy now to reduce the risk of having to tighten monetary policy excessively as I set policy to hit my inflation target," Clarke told Parliament.
Tough fiscal policy generally takes upward pressure off inflation, reducing the need for interest rate hikes.
Mariam Bell, economist at Royal Bank of Scotland said the implication of Clarke's words for monetary policy was enouraging for interest rate futures markets.
"(It is) a further short sterling positive," she said.
But Coleman said although the Chancellor claimed the budget was fiscally tight, the measures announced did not back that up.

"There are quite big cuts in personal taxation there, but a lot of the revenue-raising measures seem to be deferred into the future," he said. "It's not clear how he makes his numbers work, or how the budget is going to reduce pressure on short-term interest rates."
Clarke's inflation forecasts, too, were viewed sceptically.
The Chancellor said underlying inflation would meet the government's target of 2.5 percent, adding that he would act to curb inflationary pressure when necessary.
Analysts swiftly said the 2.5 percent inflation aim was too optimistic, particularly in combination with a growth forecast for 3.5 percent for 1997 and rising consumer spending.

"He's given away far too much to the consumer sector and the markets will struggle to try and reconcile forecasts for meeting the inflation objective when he's got consumer spending rising four percent," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica in London.
Underlying inflation staged a frightening leap in October, reaching 3.3 percent and raising the prospect that a further monetary squeeze may be needed before the year was out.
While Tuesday's budget failed to convince the market otherwise, some analysts said Clarke's prudent tax cutting and fiscal austerity should turn that view around.
"He's kept a relatively prudent budget so I would expect rates now to stay the same," said Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at Co-operative Bank in London.
"The short-end of the market has bounced a little on the back of his speech. Rates will probably stay stable until the elections," he said.
